Augustus (27 BC-14 AD), silver Denarius, Lugdunum, 15 BC, AVGVSTVS DIVI F, bare head of Augustus to right, rev. IMP X / SICIL, Diana standing front, head to right, holding spear in her right hand and bow in her left; to her lower right, dog standing left. (BMC 463. Cohen 146. RIC 173a). Ex Helmingham Hoard, Noonans 303 (18 September 2024) lot 199, very fine with a strong bust. The Helmingham Hall hoard is a Roman British coin hoard found near the grounds of Helmingham Hall around Helmingham and Stowmarket, Suffolk, dating at latest to the reign of Claudius, during the Roman conquest of Britain in the year 47 AD. Discovered in 8 September 2019, with subsequent finds in 2020-2021, the hoard consist of 748 gold and silver denarii, a blend of Iron Age, Roman Republic, Triumvirate, and Roman Imperial currency, the largest of its time, ranging from the reign of Cunobeline to Claudius. This type of Diana denarius is associated with Octavian's victory over Sextus Pompey at the Battle of Naulochus in Sicily in 36 BC. Sextus Pompey had controlled Sicily and threatened Rome's grain supplies. Octavian's general Marcus Agrippa won the decisive naval victory. Ancient tradition associated Diana with divine assistance in this success. Procopius Usurper (365-366 AD), gold solidus, Constantinople, late 365 AD, D N PROCO-PIVS P F AVG, pearl-diademed, draped and cuirassed bust right, rev. REPARATI-O FEL TEMP, Procopius standing facing, head to right, holding spear and shield; in exergue, CONS, 4.51g, 11h (RIC IX 2a; Depeyrot 14/4). Slight flan lamination at 4 o'clock on obverse, full flan and more, has beautiful lustre, slight wear on the highpoints thus almost extremely fine, extremely rare. Provenance: CNG Triton XXV (2022), 1016; Roma XVIII (2019), 1249. Procopius was the last member of the house of Constantine to don the diadem. A maternal cousin of Julian II, Procopius had a successful career as a civil servant and was made a comes, or count, after Julian won the throne in 361 AD. When Julian prepared his invasion of Persia a year later, he placed Procopius in command of a 30,000-man force intended to hook up with the allied Armenian army and join Julian's legions in Mesopotamia. Procopius later claimed that his cousin also gave him a purple cloak, along with instructions to take over as emperor should Julian be killed in battle. At any event, Procopius failed miserably in his role, contributing to the defeat of Julian's main force and his death in battle on June 27, 363 AD. When the army chose Jovian as emperor, Procopius made no protest and took Julian's body back to Tarsus for burial. But when Jovian abruptly died a few months later and the brothers Valentinian I and Valens took over, Procopius decided to make a try for the throne. While Valens was away from the capital, Procopius re-emerged at Constantinople on September 28, 365 AD, wrapped in Julian's purple cloak. The garrison proclaimed him emperor, and Procopius quickly established control of western Asia Minor. But he showed little strategic sense and soon some of his best officers and soldiers began defecting back to Valens. Meanwhile, Valens built his own forces and maneuvered Procopius into a decisive battle at Nicolea, Phrygia in May of 366 AD. Procopius suffered a crushing defeat and was summarily executed in the aftermath, ending his eight-month usurpation. The gold coinage of Procopius carries on the Constantinian tradition of fine portraiture and crisp execution. The exceptional portrait on this issue shows him wearing a close beard, probably a symbol of sympathy and mourning for his kinsman Julian II. His beard and the lack of any Christian symbolism on the reverse also hint at possible Pagan sympathies. The solidi of Procopius are particularly rare, with only 14 examples sold at auction since 1996. This is undoubtably one of the rarest Solidi from the ancient world! The obverse inscription D N PROCO-PIVS P F AVG translates to "Our Lord Procopius, Pious and Blessed Emperor." The reverse inscription translates to "REPARATI-O FEL TEMP/ CONS translates to "The restoration of happy times / Constantinople."

Good VF/EF re1507 $175 In AD 330, Constantine the Great formally dedicated Constantinople as a new imperial capital on the site of ancient Byzantium. The city occupied a strategically important position between Europe and Asia and would become the political center of the eastern Roman Empire. To commemorate the two cities, Constantine introduced a series of bronze coins honoring both Rome and Constantinople. The VRBS ROMA issues depicted the helmeted personification of Roma, while the companion CONSTANTINOPOLIS series featured the personification of the new capital. The reverse of this coin depicts one of Rome's most recognizable foundation legends: the she-wolf nursing the twins Romulus and Remus. According to Roman tradition, the twins were sons of Mars and the Vestal Virgin Rhea Silvia. Their great-uncle Amulius, fearing a challenge to his throne, ordered the infants abandoned along the Tiber River. They were discovered and nursed by a she-wolf before being raised by the shepherd Faustulus. The brothers later set out to establish a city, but a dispute over its foundation resulted in the death of Remus. Romulus became the city's first king, traditionally founding Rome in 753 BC.

EF re1505 $2500 Around AD 286–287, during the reigns of Diocletian and Maximian, a Roman naval commander named Carausius established his own imperial regime in Britain. His rise to power began with his appointment to command a fleet tasked with stopping Frankish and Saxon piracy along the coasts of northern Gaul and the English Channel. According to ancient accounts, he was accused of allowing these pirates to carry out their raids before intercepting them and keeping the recovered treasure for himself. When Maximian reportedly ordered his execution, he rebelled. Carausius presented himself as a legitimate Roman emperor, adopting traditional imperial titles and issuing coinage that closely mimicked those of Rome. His efforts to gain recognition from Diocletian and Maximian are particularly evident in a series of coins which depicts all three rulers together, accompanied by the inscription CARAUSIUS ET FRATRES SUI, meaning "Carausius and his brothers." However, neither Diocletian nor Maximian formally recognized his authority. Carausius maintained his position in Britain for approximately seven years before being assassinated in AD 293 by Allectus, one of his senior officials, who succeeded him as ruler. Roman authority was eventually restored in Britain in AD 296 following the successful campaign of Constantius Chlorus.

According to the most widespread version of the myth, Athena invented the instrument but threw it away after noticing that playing it distorted her face, and she cursed whoever should take it up. Marsyas found the pipes, mastered them, and grew confident enough to challenge Apollo, whose instrument was the lyre (or kithara), to a musical contest. The details of the contest vary. In the account preserved by Diodorus Siculus, Apollo prevailed by playing his instrument while singing, or by inverting it, a feat impossible on a wind instrument. The Muses are often named as judges, and the victor was allowed to treat the loser as he wished. Apollo had Marsyas flayed alive and his skin hung from a tree. Herodotus and Xenophon both report that the skin was displayed at Celaenae, where a river bore the satyr's name. Ovid adds that the river arose from the tears of the nymphs, satyrs, and shepherds who mourned him.

Wreathed head of Tanit left / Head of horse right; uncertain control mark or letter to right. CNP 252t (Sardinia); MAA 57f (Carthage); SNG Copenhagen 154–5 (Sardinia). Brown-green patina. Some pitting; VF. Historical Notes: This bronze coin was minted during the final decades of Carthaginian dominance in the western Mediterranean, just before the outbreak of the First Punic War (264–241 BC) against Rome. The attribution to either Carthage or Sardinia reflects the broad reach of Carthaginian influence, which extended across North Africa, Sicily, and parts of southern Europe. • The obverse features Tanit, the principal goddess of Carthage, associated with fertility, protection, and the moon. Her wreathed portrait reflects Hellenistic artistic influence and underscores her central role in Punic religion and civic identity. • The reverse horse head is one of the most iconic symbols of Carthaginian coinage. It likely represents the famed Numidian cavalry or the sacred status of horses in Punic culture. Horses were vital to Carthage’s military success and trade networks. • The uncertain control mark beside the horse may indicate a specific minting authority or workshop, though its exact meaning remains debated among scholars. • If minted in Sardinia, this coin would have served both as currency and a political statement, asserting Carthaginian control over the island’s strategic ports and resources. Sardinia was a contested territory, and coinage helped reinforce Carthage’s presence. • The dating places this issue in the pre-Hannibalic era, when Carthage was a powerful maritime empire rivaling Rome. These coins circulated widely and were used to pay mercenaries, fund trade, and support colonial administration. This AE Shekel stands as a tangible link to Carthage’s imperial ambitions and its rich blend of Punic and Hellenistic traditions—an artifact from the brink of one of antiquity’s greatest conflicts.

164LF4Z) PTOLEMAIC KINGS of EGYPT. Ptolemy II Philadelphos. 285-246 BC. AE Diobol (29.5mm, 22.36 g, 12h). Alexandreia mint. Series 3, circa late 260s–246 BC. Horned head of Zeus-Ammon right, wearing tainia with basileion / Eagle with closed wings standing left on thunderbolt; E between legs. CPE B225a; Svoronos 449; SNG Copenhagen –. Rough red-brown surfaces, with patches of green. VF. Historical Note: This large bronze diobol was struck during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphos (285-246 BC) , the second ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt and one of the most influential Hellenistic monarchs. Under his rule, Alexandria flourished as a center of commerce, learning, and culture, housing the renowned Library and Mouseion. The portrait of Zeus-Ammon , a syncretic fusion of the Greek Zeus and the Egyptian god Amun, reflects the Ptolemies' policy of blending Greek and Egyptian religious traditions to reinforce their legitimacy among both populations. The reverse eagle standing upon a thunderbolt became the enduring dynastic emblem of the Ptolemaic Kingdom and appeared on its coinage for nearly three centuries. Large bronze denominations such as this diobol formed the backbone of Egypt's closed monetary system, which circulated primarily within the kingdom's borders and supported its highly centralized economy. Series 3 issues , to which this coin belongs, were produced during the later years of Ptolemy II's reign, a period marked by Egypt's naval strength, expanding trade networks, and continued rivalry with the Seleucid Empire during the Syrian Wars. The control letter E between the eagle's legs served as a mint control mark used for production accountability within the Alexandrian mint.

SC 2034.2a; HGC 9, 1061. Good Very  Fine A military commander and leading supporter of the usurper Alexander I Balas, Diodotos placed Antiochos VI on the Seleukid throne following Balas' death. Two years later, upon the death of the young king, Diodotos took the throne himself, supposedly upon the acclamation of his troops. Unlike previous usurpers, Diodotos did not fabricate his lineage into the Seleukid house, but maintained that the Seleukid line had ended, and his was the beginning of a new era. He broke tradition by assuming the title autocrat rather than king, and took the name Tryphon ('the magnificent'). His reign proved very unpopular, and a new Seleukid claimant, Antiochos VII Sidetes, rose against him. Within three years Tryphon was defeated and killed.

The joint rule of the ambitious Nabataean minister Syllaeus and his youthful and eventual successor Aretas IV produced a power struggle which lasted into their fourth year, corresponding to 6 BC. Coinage is thought to have been produced more neutrally at first, with the portrait of Obodas III, their predecessor, placed on many of the issues.
